15.title: ever-rising spirits
15.hook: ever-rising spirits — optimism as a discipline
15.tomorrow: what a sikh carries and why
15.howItsDone: Sikhs speak of chardi kala in everyday greetings and answers, and ask for it at the close of the Ardas prayer; it is taught as a lasting optimism rooted in trust in God's will.

screen: `DAY FIFTEEN.`

segments.voice: Last week closed at the gurdwara, the door of the Guru. Your line was cover your head, take off your shoes, come in. Did you find the nearest one? Day fifteen, and the last week of camp one.
screen: `THE GURDWARA — COME IN.`

segments.voice: Ask a Sikh grandfather how he's doing. He's eighty-one, his knees are bad, he's just come back from the hospital, and the doctor's news wasn't great. There's a decent chance he'll smile and say two words: chardi kala. Not I'm fine. Not can't complain. Something more like: spirits rising. It can sound almost stubborn, and in a way it is. It isn't that he hasn't noticed his knees or the doctor's news. He's noticed everything. He's just decided which way his spirit is going to face. Today, a word Sikhs treat not as a mood that visits you, but as a discipline you practice.
screen: `BAD KNEES, HARD NEWS.` → `CHARDI KALA.` → `NOT A MOOD. A DISCIPLINE.`

segments.voice: Chardi kala. Chardi means rising, climbing, ascending. Kala means spirit, energy, state of being. Ever-rising spirits. Relentless optimism. Hope that keeps getting up. Here's the difference between chardi kala and just being cheerful. Cheerfulness depends on circumstances. Chardi kala is meant to hold when circumstances collapse. And Sikh history has asked a great deal of it. There were long stretches, especially in the eighteenth century, when Sikhs were hunted, driven into forests and hills, with prices on their heads. Out of those years came a whole defiant way of speaking. Tradition remembers that a lone Sikh might call himself sava lakh, a hundred and twenty-five thousand: one man, a whole army. That isn't denial. It's a refusal to let the circumstances write your spirit for you. Where does it come from? From trust. Sikhs speak of hukam, the will or order of God running through everything. If all of life, even the hard parts, is held inside the one, then despair doesn't get the last word. Chardi kala is what that trust looks like from the outside. And you'll hear the phrase every time Sikhs finish their communal prayer, the Ardas, which we'll open in a few days. Near its very end, it asks for exactly this: through Nanak, may the name, and the spirit, be ever-rising. One more thing. Chardi kala isn't pretending the pain isn't there. Sikhs grieve. Sikhs weep. The word doesn't forbid sadness. It just keeps pointing up, like a plant that grows toward the light even in a dark room. Optimism, practiced, not merely felt.
screen: `CHARDI — RISING. KALA — SPIRIT.` · `NOT CHEERFULNESS. IT HOLDS WHEN THINGS FALL.` · `ONE SIKH, A WHOLE ARMY.` · `TRUST IN HUKAM, THE WILL OF GOD.` · then, large: `EVER-RISING SPIRITS.`

segments.voice: Settle, and let one heavy thing come to mind, something that's actually hard right now. Don't push it away. Look at it honestly. Then, without denying any of it, let your posture rise a little: lift your chest, soften your face, breathe in as if you're drawing yourself upward. You're not saying it's fine. You're choosing which way your spirit faces. Stay there, with the weight and the rising together. The bell holds the time.
Chardi kala. Ever-rising spirits: hope practiced as a discipline, holding even when life is hard. Fifteenth word.
screen: `CHARDI KALA — your 15th word`.

segments.voice: Your line: rise anyway. Today, when something goes wrong, notice it fully, then do one small thing that faces up. Day fifteen.

16.title: what a sikh carries and why
16.hook: what a Sikh carries and why
16.tomorrow: the tenth guru, the khalsa, the saint-soldier
16.howItsDone: Sikhs initiated into the Khalsa keep the five Ks at all times: uncut hair, a wooden comb, a steel bracelet, a cotton undergarment and a small sword. Many other Sikhs wear the kara.

screen: `DAY SIXTEEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: chardi kala, ever-rising spirits. Your line was rise anyway. When something went wrong, which way did you face? Day sixteen.
screen: `CHARDI KALA — RISE ANYWAY.`

segments.voice: A wedding ring, turned on the finger during a hard meeting. A photo in a wallet. A string tied around a wrist. A grandmother's watch that doesn't even keep time anymore. Small things people carry to remember. They don't do anything, exactly. But touch one, and something comes back: a promise, a person, who someone meant to be. Initiated Sikhs carry five of those, all day, every day, each one tied to something different. Today: what a Sikh carries, and why.
screen: `A RING, A PHOTO, A STRING.` → `TOUCH IT, AND SOMETHING COMES BACK.` → `A SIKH CARRIES FIVE.`

segments.voice: They're called the five Ks, because in Punjabi each one begins with the sound k. Sikhs who have been initiated into the Khalsa, the community of the committed, keep all five. The tradition traces them to the tenth Guru, Guru Gobind Singh, whom you'll meet tomorrow. One. Kesh: uncut hair, which you met on day twelve under the turban. Accepting the body as it was made. Two. Kanga: a small wooden comb, tucked into the hair. Keep the hair clean and ordered, and the life too. Three. Kara: a plain steel bracelet on the wrist. A circle, with no beginning and no end, like the one God. Sikhs often say that when your hand reaches for something, the kara is there first, asking: is this something a Sikh's hand should do? Four. Kachera: a cotton undergarment, like simple shorts. Self-restraint, and readiness to move. Five. Kirpan: a small sword, worn in a sheath, often under the clothes. It's a symbol of the duty to protect people who can't protect themselves, and of dignity and courage; it isn't there for aggression. Notice something about all five. None is a decoration. Each is plain, practical, ordinary: a comb, a bracelet, underwear, hair. That's the point. The reminders aren't locked in a temple. They're on the body, all day, at work, in the shower, at the gym. Faith you can touch. And for Sikhs who aren't initiated, the kara especially is widely worn, a single steel circle that says the same thing: remember.
screen: `FIVE THINGS THAT BEGIN WITH K.` · `KESH AND KANGA — HAIR, AND ITS COMB.` · `KARA — THE HAND REMEMBERS.` · `KACHERA AND KIRPAN — RESTRAINT, PROTECTION.` · then, large: `FAITH YOU CAN TOUCH.`

segments.voice: Choose one thing you're wearing or carrying right now: a ring, a watch, a hair tie, your sleeve. Put your hand on it. Decide, just for today, what it's going to remind you of: something you believe, a person, a promise. Close your hand around it and breathe with that meaning for a while. Let the object and the reminder become one thing. The bell holds the time.
The five Ks. Kesh, kanga, kara, kachera, kirpan: five reminders a committed Sikh carries every day. Sixteenth word.
screen: `THE FIVE KS — your 16th word`.

segments.voice: Your line: reminders you can touch. Each time you touch the thing you chose today, let it bring its reminder back. Day sixteen.

17.title: the tenth guru, the khalsa, the saint-soldier
17.hook: the tenth Guru, the Khalsa, the saint-soldier
17.howItsDone: Sikhs honor Guru Gobind Singh as the tenth Guru and founder of the Khalsa, celebrate his birth each year, recite his compositions in daily prayers, and speak of the ideal of the sant sipahi, the saint-soldier.

screen: `DAY SEVENTEEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: the five Ks, from the uncut hair to the steel kara. Your line was reminders you can touch. What did the thing you chose remind you of? Day seventeen.
screen: `THE FIVE KS — REMINDERS YOU CAN TOUCH.`

segments.voice: Nine years old. A father leaving home, knowing he may not come back. He has gone to the capital to stand up for the right of people from another faith to practice theirs. And he doesn't come back. He's executed. Now the community turns to the boy and tells him: you are the Guru. That's how the tenth Guru's leadership began, in 1675, as Sikh tradition tells it. The boy grew into a poet, a warrior, a writer in several languages, and the founder of the Khalsa. He carried a sword, and he wrote devotional poetry that Sikhs still recite in their daily prayers. Today, the Guru who held both.
screen: `NINE YEARS OLD.` → `A FATHER WHO DOESN'T COME BACK.` → `YOU ARE THE GURU.`

segments.voice: Guru Gobind Singh, born in 1666 by the traditional dating, the tenth and last human Guru of the Sikhs. His father was the ninth Guru, Guru Tegh Bahadur. Sikh tradition remembers that Guru Tegh Bahadur went to Delhi on behalf of Hindu Kashmiri pandits who were being pressed to convert, and was executed there by the Mughal authorities. Sikhs honor him as a martyr who gave his life for the freedom of others to worship. That memory shaped his son. Guru Gobind Singh taught that a person of faith should be two things at once. The Sikh phrase for it is sant sipahi: saint and soldier. Saint, because the inner life comes first: remembrance, humility, the name. Soldier, because when the weak are being crushed, a saint doesn't just look away. The sword on day sixteen, the kirpan, comes from exactly this. And the order matters. The saint comes first. A soldier with no saint in him is only violence. A saint with no courage may stand by while others suffer. In 1699, tradition says, at a great gathering at Anandpur, the Guru founded the Khalsa, the community of the initiated, the ones who keep the five Ks. It's a dramatic story, and we'll tell it properly later in the year. He lost his father, and all four of his sons, to the violence of his time, and he's still remembered for chardi kala, rising spirits. And near the end of his life he made a decision that changed everything: there would be no eleventh human Guru. We'll come to that in three days.
screen: `THE TENTH AND LAST HUMAN GURU.` · `A FATHER WHO DIED FOR OTHERS' FREEDOM.` · `SANT SIPAHI — SAINT AND SOLDIER.` · `THE SAINT COMES FIRST.` · then, large: `SWORD AND SAINT.`

segments.voice: Settle and breathe. Let one of your hands rest open on your lap: that's the saint, quiet, open, remembering. Let the other close into a gentle fist: that's the courage to stand up for someone. Feel both at once. Now think of one person in your life who might need you to stand up for them. Just hold them in mind, with both hands. The bell holds the time.
Guru Gobind Singh. The tenth Guru, founder of the Khalsa, poet and warrior: the saint-soldier. Seventeenth word.
screen: `GURU GOBIND SINGH — your 17th word`.

segments.voice: Your line: sword and saint. Today, speak up once for someone who can't easily speak up for themselves, gently and without fear. Day seventeen.

18.title: the stories of the gurus
18.hook: the stories of the Gurus — Nanak and the rich man's needle
18.carry: what will you take with you?
18.howItsDone: Sikhs tell sakhis about the Gurus to children at home and in gurdwara classes, and preachers retell them during services to draw out a teaching.

screen: `DAY EIGHTEEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Guru Gobind Singh, the saint-soldier. Your line was sword and saint. Who did you speak up for? Day eighteen.
screen: `GURU GOBIND SINGH — SWORD AND SAINT.`

segments.voice: Every family has its stories. The time grandpa drove the wrong way for three hours. The time your aunt told off a bank manager. Told at weddings, at funerals, at the kitchen table, until the kids can recite them word for word. Nobody checks them against a record. That's not what they're for. They're for knowing who you are. Sikh families have stories like that about the Gurus, told to children at bedtime and to adults in the gurdwara. They're short, often funny, often sharp. Today, the word for those stories, and one of them: a rich man, and a needle.
screen: `EVERY FAMILY HAS ITS STORIES.` → `TOLD UNTIL THE KIDS CAN RECITE THEM.` → `A RICH MAN, AND A NEEDLE.`

segments.voice: Sakhi. A story, and also a testimony, a witness's account: this is what was seen. The sakhis are the stories of the Gurus' lives, and the collections about Guru Nanak's life are called janamsakhis, life-stories, written down in the generations after he died, in several versions that don't always agree. Sikhs hold them with love. Historians read them as devotional stories more than as records; in the telling, what matters is what each one teaches. Here's the needle. The story says Nanak came to Lahore, where a very rich man named Duni Chand lived. Tradition says he flew flags over his house, one for each great sum of money he'd piled up. He invited Nanak to a feast and showed off everything. Before leaving, Nanak handed him a small sewing needle. Keep this for me, he said, and give it back to me in the next world. Duni Chand took it proudly and went to tell his wife. She looked at the needle, and at him, and asked the obvious question. How exactly are you going to take a needle with you when you die? And Duni Chand stood there holding it. If he couldn't carry a needle, what about the flags, the gold, the house? He went back to Nanak, the story says, and asked what he should do. And he began to share his wealth with people who needed it. That's the shape of a sakhi. No lecture. Just one small object, one question, and a man who suddenly sees his whole life differently. We'll come back to this story later on the path. For now, just the needle.
screen: `SAKHI — A STORY, A WITNESS.` · `LOVED, NOT ALWAYS A RECORD.` · `KEEP THIS NEEDLE FOR ME.` · `HOW WILL YOU TAKE IT WITH YOU?` · then, large: `ONE OBJECT, ONE QUESTION.`

segments.voice: Hold something small in your hand, a coin, a key, a paperclip, or just imagine a needle resting in your palm. Look at it. Now ask Duni Chand's wife's question, gently, about your own life: what am I carrying that I can't take with me? And what could I take with me: kindness given, love shared, truth told? Sit with the needle and the question. The bell holds the time.
The sakhis. The stories of the Gurus, told to witness what they taught, like the rich man's needle. Eighteenth word.
screen: `THE SAKHIS — your 18th word`.

segments.voice: Your line: what will you take with you? Today, before you buy or keep something, ask it once. Day eighteen.

19.title: the standing prayer
19.hook: the standing prayer; "sarbat da bhala" — the good of all
19.tomorrow: a scripture that is the guru
19.howItsDone: Sikhs stand with palms joined, facing the Guru Granth Sahib, while one person leads the Ardas at the end of services and before important events; it closes by asking for chardi kala and sarbat da bhala, the good of all.

screen: `DAY NINETEEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: the sakhis, and the rich man's needle. Your line was what will you take with you? Did you ask it before you bought something? Day nineteen.
screen: `THE SAKHIS — WHAT WILL YOU TAKE WITH YOU?`

segments.voice: Please let my kid be okay. Please let me get the job. Please protect us. When things are hard, a prayer can shrink to the size of a family: mine, ours, our side. Now a room full of Sikhs at the end of a service. Everyone rises to their feet. Palms pressed together. One person leads a prayer that everyone knows, recalling the Gurus and the martyrs, asking for help with this family's wedding or that one's illness. And then, in its very last line, it widens out, past the room, past the community, to everyone. Today, the standing prayer.
screen: `PLEASE, FOR MY OWN.` → `A ROOM RISES TO ITS FEET.` → `THE LAST LINE WIDENS OUT.`

segments.voice: Ardas. It comes from a Persian word for a petition, a humble request. It's the prayer Sikhs offer standing, facing the Guru Granth Sahib, at the end of services, before a journey, at weddings and funerals, at the start of almost anything important. Ardas has a shape. It opens with verses by Guru Gobind Singh remembering the Gurus, one by one, from Nanak on. Then it remembers: the scripture, the five beloved ones of the Khalsa, the Guru's sons, the men and women who suffered and gave their lives for their faith. It's a prayer with a long memory. Then, in the middle, it becomes personal. The one leading it adds the day's particular requests: a new baby, a sick grandmother, a family moving house, thanks for a harvest. So no two Ardas are exactly the same. And then the end, which is always the same. It asks for chardi kala, the ever-rising spirits of day fifteen, and then three words: sarbat da bhala. The good of all. Not the good of Sikhs. Not the good of the people in this room. The good of everyone, everywhere. In the plain sense of the words, that includes people who've never heard of the Gurus, and people who've wronged the community. In a prayer that remembers so much suffering, that's a remarkable place to end. All that memory, and the final request is for the well-being of the whole world. Then the congregation calls out together, the same greeting from day two: Waheguru ji ka Khalsa, Waheguru ji ki fateh. And they sit down.
screen: `ARDAS — A HUMBLE REQUEST, STANDING.` · `A PRAYER WITH A LONG MEMORY.` · `THE DAY'S OWN REQUESTS.` · `SARBAT DA BHALA — THE GOOD OF ALL.` · then, large: `FOR EVERYONE, NOT JUST US.`

segments.voice: If you can, stand up. Let your feet settle and your hands come together in front of your chest. First, bring to mind the people closest to you. Then widen it: your street, your town, strangers on the other side of the world. Then widen it again, to someone you find hard to love. Hold all of them together. If you pray, you can say three words from the Ardas: sarbat da bhala. If not, just stand there wishing them well. The bell holds the time.
Ardas. The standing prayer, a humble request that remembers the past and ends asking for the good of all. Nineteenth word.
screen: `ARDAS — your 19th word`.

segments.voice: Your line: for everyone, not just us. Today, wish someone well who isn't on your side: a rival, another team, a stranger in the news. Day nineteen.

20.title: a scripture that is the guru
20.hook: a scripture that is the Guru; why it's carried, covered, put to bed
20.howItsDone: In every gurdwara the Guru Granth Sahib rests under a canopy on a raised platform, is attended with a chaur, opened at dawn and put to rest at night; a hymn read at random each morning is taken as the day's hukamnama.

screen: `DAY TWENTY.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ardas, the standing prayer, ending in sarbat da bhala. Your line was for everyone, not just us. Who did you wish well? Day twenty.
screen: `ARDAS — FOR EVERYONE, NOT JUST US.`

segments.voice: Late evening at a gurdwara. The last hymn has been sung. Someone gently closes a very large book, wraps it in embroidered cloth, and lifts it onto their head. Others walk ahead, sometimes calling out, while someone waves a whisk of long white hair over it, the way attendants once did for a king. The book is carried in procession to its own room, laid on a bed, and covered for the night. At dawn it's carried back out, unwrapped and opened, and the day begins. If you've never seen this, it can look astonishing. Why would anyone put a book to bed? Because on this path, the book isn't just a book. Today: a scripture that is the Guru.
screen: `A LARGE BOOK, WRAPPED IN CLOTH.` → `CARRIED ON SOMEONE'S HEAD.` → `PUT TO BED FOR THE NIGHT.`

segments.voice: The Guru Granth Sahib. Granth means book. Sahib is a word of deep respect. And Guru, the teacher you met on day two. The Guru who is a book. Here's how that happened. The fifth Guru, Guru Arjan, gathered the hymns of the Gurus before him and his own, and in 1604 installed the collection at the Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar. Then, three days ago, we met Guru Gobind Singh. Near the end of his life, in 1708, the tenth Guru declared that there would be no more human Gurus. From then on, Sikhs would find their Guru in the scripture. So when Sikhs bow before it, they're bowing to the Guru, present in the words. That's why it's treated the way you'd treat a revered teacher in the room. It sits higher than everyone, on a small platform under a canopy. It's covered with cloth. Someone attends it with a whisk. It's put to rest at night and brought out at dawn. And inside? About fourteen hundred pages, which Sikhs call angs, limbs, as if of a body. Hymns by six of the Gurus. And, remarkably, hymns by holy poets who weren't Sikhs at all: Kabir, a weaver; Ravidas, from a caste many looked down on; Sheikh Farid, a Muslim Sufi. Their words sit in the scripture beside the Gurus'. Almost all of it is poetry, arranged by musical mode, meant to be sung. Every morning, many gurdwaras open it at random and read the first hymn on the page. It's called the hukamnama, the order of the day. Sikhs don't only read this book. They listen to it, as to someone speaking to them today.
screen: `GRANTH — BOOK. SAHIB — RESPECT.` · `1708: NO MORE HUMAN GURUS.` · `TREATED LIKE A TEACHER IN THE ROOM.` · `GURUS AND SAINTS, SIDE BY SIDE.` · then, large: `A LIVING BOOK.`

segments.voice: Think of words that have spoken to you, a line from a book, a letter, something someone once said that you've never forgotten. Bring it to mind as exactly as you can. Now imagine those words not as something printed, but as someone sitting beside you, saying them to you now, today. Let them speak. Just listen. The bell holds the time.
The Guru Granth Sahib. The Sikh scripture, honored as the living Guru since 1708, holding the Gurus' hymns and the words of other saints. Twentieth word.

21.title: the mountain ahead
21.hook: the mountain ahead; Nanak's morning prayer
21.howItsDone: Sikhs who keep the daily prayers recite Japji Sahib each morning, often before dawn after bathing, as the first of them; children often learn it by heart a stanza at a time.

screen: `DAY TWENTY-ONE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Guru Granth Sahib, the scripture that is the Guru. Your line was a living book. Which line spoke to you? Day twenty-one, the last day of camp one.
screen: `THE GURU GRANTH SAHIB — A LIVING BOOK.`

segments.voice: It's still dark outside. Four in the morning, maybe five. In homes across Punjab, and in London, Toronto, California, Nairobi, someone is already up. They've bathed. They sit quietly, cover their head, and begin to recite, often from memory, a long poem. They'll do the same tomorrow, and the day after, for their whole lives. Some learned it as children, a verse at a time, sitting beside a grandparent before school. It's the first thing in the scripture and the first thing in their day. You've been standing at the foot of it for three weeks without knowing. Today, the mountain ahead.
screen: `FOUR IN THE MORNING.` → `A LONG POEM, FROM MEMORY.` → `THE FIRST THING IN THE DAY.`

segments.voice: Japji Sahib. Jap, to recite, to repeat, the same root as naam japna. Ji and Sahib, words of love and respect. It's Guru Nanak's great poem, and it opens the Guru Granth Sahib. It begins with the root verse you learned on days five and six. Then a short verse that the translator Macauliffe gave like this: "The True One was in the beginning; the True One was in the primal age." Then come thirty-eight stanzas, called pauris, steps or rungs, like a ladder. And a closing verse that pictures air as the Guru, water as the father, and the earth as the great mother of all. Inside, it's full of questions. How can you think your way to God? You can't, the first stanza says, not if you think a hundred thousand times. Silence won't do it, and piling up possessions won't. What will? Living within hukam, God's will, the word you met on day fifteen. Later stanzas marvel at creation beyond counting, and describe realms a soul climbs through. It's a mountain of a poem. That's why your line is a promise. Later on this path, we'll climb Japji verse by verse, one stanza at a time. And look how far you've come already. Seva, Waheguru, Nanak, Ik Onkar. The root verse, both lines. Simran, langar, kirat karni, vand chakna, naam japna. The turban, sangat, the gurdwara. Chardi kala, the five Ks, Guru Gobind Singh, the sakhis, Ardas, the Guru Granth Sahib. And now Japji. Twenty-one words. Camp one is done. Tomorrow camp two begins: the stories, starting with a baby born in a small village in 1469.
screen: `JAP — TO RECITE.` · `THE TRUE ONE WAS IN THE BEGINNING.` · `THIRTY-EIGHT STEPS, LIKE A LADDER.` · `TWENTY-ONE WORDS. CAMP ONE DONE.` · then, large: `THE MOUNTAIN AHEAD.`

segments.voice: Sit tall, the way someone sits in the early morning to recite. Picture a mountain path ahead of you, thirty-eight steps rising into the light. You don't have to climb today. Just stand at the bottom and look up. Then look back down the path you've already walked: twenty-one days, twenty-one words. Breathe with both, what's behind and what's ahead. The bell holds the time.
Japji Sahib. Guru Nanak's morning poem, the first in the scripture: the root verse, thirty-eight stanzas and a closing verse. Twenty-first word.
screen: `JAPJI SAHIB — your 21st word`.

segments.voice: Your line: 38 stanzas, verse by verse. Tomorrow morning, before your phone, give the first minute of the day to something that matters. Camp two starts tomorrow: the stories. Day twenty-one.

screen: `DAY 21 COUNTS.` → `CAMP ONE COMPLETE.` → `TOMORROW: BORN AT TALWANDI, 1469.`
